title: AI Unlocked: Agriculture & Agribusiness
blurb: For farmers, cooperatives, and agripreneurs: advisory and diagnostic tools in the field, market and price intelligence, farm-business automation, precision-ag realities by budget level, and climate-smart planning — built for African and global contexts alike.

modules.t: AI on the Farm: The Real Map
modules.d: What AI can actually do for smallholders, cooperatives and agribusinesses — and what it cannot.
modules.body:
Separating promise from reality

Agricultural AI is often presented through images of drones, robots and sensors on large mechanised farms. For most farmers in Cameroon and across Africa — smallholders cultivating a few hectares of cocoa, coffee, maize, cassava, plantain, vegetables or livestock — the reality is different: a mobile phone (often basic), intermittent connectivity, limited access to extension officers, credit and reliable markets. The most valuable AI for these farmers is usually not robotics but information: diagnosis, advice, prices, weather and business support delivered through the phone.

The agricultural value chain

AI can contribute at each stage: inputs (choosing seed varieties, fertiliser recommendations), production (planting decisions, pest and disease diagnosis, irrigation), post-harvest (storage, loss reduction, quality grading), processing and value addition, marketing (price information, buyer matching), and finance and risk (credit scoring, insurance, record-keeping). Cooperatives and agribusinesses can also use AI for planning, logistics, quality management, traceability and reporting.

The extension gap. In many countries, each public extension officer is expected to serve hundreds or thousands of farmers, so most farmers rarely receive timely advice. AI-supported advisory — via apps, SMS, voice and chat — can extend the reach of agronomic knowledge, especially when it supports rather than replaces extension workers and lead farmers who know local conditions.

What AI does well in agriculture

  • Recognising some pests and diseases from photos, where well trained on local crops.
  • Answering agronomic questions and explaining good practices in local languages, when grounded in reliable sources.
  • Summarising weather forecasts and market information into actionable advice.
  • Helping farmers and cooperatives keep records, calculate costs and write business plans and loan applications.
  • Analysing satellite imagery for crop monitoring at larger scales.

What AI does poorly — or dangerously

  • Giving generic advice that ignores local soils, varieties, climate and regulations.
  • Recommending pesticide products or doses without regard to local registration, safety or correct use — a serious health and environmental risk.
  • Diagnosing diseases it was not trained on, or from poor-quality photos, with false confidence.
  • Working in many local languages and accents.
  • Replacing trust built through demonstration plots, peer farmers and extension relationships.

Who benefits — and who is left out

Digital agriculture can widen inequality if only better-connected, literate, male and wealthier farmers benefit. Women farmers often have less access to phones, data, training and credit. Designs that use voice, local languages, group-based delivery through cooperatives and community intermediaries help reach those otherwise excluded.

A practical stance

Treat AI as an assistant to good agronomy and good business: it helps you find and apply knowledge faster, but local verification — with extension officers, research institutes such as IRAD in Cameroon, and experienced farmers — remains essential.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my agricultural AI advisor. Ask me about my role (farmer, cooperative, agribusiness, extension), crops or livestock, location, farm size, phone access and biggest challenges. Map where AI could help across my value chain, rank three opportunities by value and feasibility, and for each tell me what must be verified locally and with whom.

Going deeper — choosing the right AI problem on the farm

Before choosing any tool, a farmer, cooperative or agribusiness should be able to answer one question: what decision will this help me make better, and when? Agricultural AI creates value only when it improves a real decision — what to plant, when to plant, whether a crop is diseased, when to sell, whether to borrow — at the moment that decision is made.

The decision-calendar framework. Draw your farming year as a calendar and mark the key decisions: land preparation, variety and input choice, planting date, pest and disease scouting, fertiliser timing, harvest, storage, sale and repayment. For each decision, note (1) what information you currently use, (2) what goes wrong most often, and (3) what information would change the decision. AI is worth exploring only where the third column has a clear answer and the information can reach you in time, through a channel you can use — voice, SMS, WhatsApp or an app.

A fit test for any tool. Ask five questions: Is it trained or tested on my crops and region? Does it work on my phone and network, including offline? Is it in a language I or my members understand? Who stands behind the advice — a research institute, ministry, NGO or company — and can I verify it with an extension officer? What happens to my data?

Worked example. A cocoa farmer in the Centre Region lists her decisions and finds the costliest problem is black pod disease spreading during the rainy season, because she sprays too late. The useful information is early warning: rainfall forecasts plus regular scouting. Her plan: receive weather forecasts by SMS or app, scout the farm twice a week during wet periods, photograph suspicious pods and check them with an advisory tool, then confirm with the cooperative's extension contact before buying any fungicide. She records the dates and results to compare with last season.

Pitfalls. Adopting a tool because it is impressive, not because it serves a decision; trusting a diagnosis app trained on crops from another continent; following chemical recommendations without checking registration, dose and safety equipment; and forgetting that many farmers, especially women and older farmers, may share a phone or lack data credit. Projects that ignore these realities rarely last beyond the pilot.

Start small. Pick one decision, one season and one simple measure of success — for example, percentage of crop lost to a specific disease, or price received compared with the market average. Evidence from your own farm is more persuasive to neighbours than any advertisement.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as an agricultural extension adviser for [crop] farming in [region, country]. Help me build my decision calendar: ask me about my farming year, then list my key decisions month by month, the information I currently use, what often goes wrong, and where AI-supported information (weather, diagnosis, prices, records) could help. Recommend one decision to focus on this season and a simple way to measure the result. Mark anything I must confirm with a local extension officer.

📚 Glossary

  • Smallholder: farmer cultivating a small area, often with family labour
  • Extension services: advisory services that share agricultural knowledge with farmers
  • Value chain: sequence from inputs through production to market
  • Lead farmer: experienced farmer who demonstrates practices to peers

📖 References

  • FAO — Digital agriculture and e-agriculture resources.
  • CTA & Dalberg (2019). The Digitalisation of African Agriculture Report 2018–2019.
  • IRAD (Institute of Agricultural Research for Development), Cameroon.
  • World Bank — ICT in Agriculture Sourcebook.

quiz.q: A cocoa cooperative near Mbalmayo has 600 members, most with basic phones and weak signal, and a USD 15,000 grant for digital tools. Which investment is most likely to create value first?
opts: A smartphone diagnosis app for all members, with handsets bought from the grant for each family
Two survey drones to map every member's plot each season for yield and canopy estimates
SMS and voice advice on disease, weather and prices, linked to lead farmers and extension
A satellite crop-monitoring subscription giving the board weekly vegetation maps of the area
quiz.x: Phone-delivered information fits basic phones and weak signal and reaches all 600 members. Satellite monitoring is a defensible runner-up for a cooperative but serves the board, not most members' daily decisions.

quiz.q: A chatbot tells a maize farmer in Bafoussam to spray a named insecticide at 2 L/ha against fall armyworm. The product name is unfamiliar to the local agro-dealer. What is the best next step?
opts: Buy the closest similar product the agro-dealer stocks and apply it at the 2 L/ha rate suggested
Check with the extension officer that it is registered in Cameroon and the dose is right first
Apply half the suggested rate on a small test strip first and watch the results for a week
Ask two other chatbots for a second opinion and spray if at least two of them agree on the dose
quiz.x: Pesticide advice must be checked for local registration, dose and safety with a qualified person. A test strip feels cautious but still uses an unverified product and dose, which is the core risk.

quiz.q: In a district of Adamawa, one public extension officer covers about 2,000 farmers. A ministry official proposes an AI advisory app. Which design best matches what the module teaches about the extension gap?
opts: Equip the officer and lead farmers with the app so they can advise more farmers and verify unclear cases
Keep the officer's current visit schedule and offer the app on request to farmers who can pay for it
Give the app directly to farmers and redeploy the officer to administrative tasks in the town office
Use the app to rank farmers by yield so the officer visits the highest-producing farms first each month
quiz.x: AI extends reach best when it supports extension workers and lead farmers who know local conditions. Offering it to paying farmers leaves the gap unaddressed and widens inequality.

quiz.q: A coffee buyer in Dschang finds that after harvest, beans lose weight and quality in damp village stores before they reach the exporter. At which value-chain stage should an AI tool be aimed first?
opts: Production: disease diagnosis on coffee leaves to prevent berry diseases in the field
Marketing: buyer matching to find exporters paying higher prices for the same beans
Inputs: variety selection to plant types with naturally lower moisture at harvest time
Post-harvest: drying and storage advice, moisture alerts and grading before sale
quiz.x: The loss happens in storage, so post-harvest tools address the actual problem. Marketing is a runner-up, but better buyers do not fix beans spoiling before they arrive.

quiz.q: A women's vegetable group in Bamenda shares two basic phones among 40 members, several of whom do not read well. An NGO wants to deliver AI advice. Which design is most inclusive?
opts: Printed monthly summaries of AI advice in French, read aloud by the secretary at meetings
An image-diagnosis smartphone app installed on the two phones and held by the group leader
Voice messages in Pidgin and local languages played and discussed at weekly group meetings
A text-based WhatsApp chatbot in English that members can query on the group phones in turn
quiz.x: Voice, local languages and group-based delivery reach members with limited phones and literacy. Printed French summaries use the group but still exclude those who do not follow French.

quiz.q: A US agtech firm pitches Cameroonian cocoa farmers a disease-ID app with 95% accuracy, measured on cocoa photos from Ecuador and Ghana. What should a cooperative manager conclude?
opts: Use it, but just for diseases that also occur in Ecuador and Ghana, trusting the scores there
Test it on local varieties, diseases and phone photos before relying on it for field decisions
Accept it, since 95% accuracy on two other cocoa regions shows it handles cocoa disease well
Reject it, because tools developed outside Africa cannot recognise diseases on local farms
quiz.x: Accuracy depends on training data; a tool can be confidently wrong on local conditions. Limiting use to shared diseases is reasonable-sounding but still assumes local photos and varieties behave the same.

quiz.q: A cassava processor in Ebolowa wants to use AI this year. She has records in notebooks, struggles to get a bank loan, and loses money when gari prices drop at harvest. Which use is most realistic first?
opts: Use satellite imagery to estimate the cassava supply of her suppliers before buying roots
Install moisture sensors in cassava fields to time harvest for the best starch content each year
Commission a custom machine-learning model that forecasts gari prices across regional markets
Turn her notebook records into cost tables and a business plan to support a loan application
quiz.x: Records, costs and business plans are tasks AI does well for small businesses and directly address her finance problem. A price model targets a real problem but is costly and unproven at her scale.

quiz.q: A Kenyan-style agri-advisory start-up plans to enter Cameroon. Which lesson from M-Pesa's rural spread (launched 2007) should most shape its product?
opts: Deliver services through phones people already own, including basic handsets, at low cost
Build a premium smartphone app and wait for handset prices to fall before going rural
Partner first with large mechanised farms, then let the model trickle down to smallholders
Focus on robotics demonstrations to build trust before launching any information service
quiz.x: M-Pesa showed phone-based services reach rural people at scale. Starting with large farms is a familiar growth strategy but misses where most farmers are.

quiz.q: A lead farmer in Kumba receives AI advice on plantain spacing that conflicts with what IRAD trials and older farmers in the village recommend. How should she handle it?
opts: Discuss both with the extension officer and trial the AI idea on a small demo plot first
Follow the AI advice, since it draws on more global research than local farmers can read
Drop the AI advice and rely on village practice, as AI rarely fits Cameroonian conditions
Split the farm in half and follow each recommendation fully to see which works better
quiz.x: Local verification with experts and a small trial balances new ideas against local knowledge. Splitting the whole farm tests the idea but risks half the harvest on unverified advice.

quiz.q: An agribusiness in Douala plans an AI farm-records app for its 3,000 outgrowers. FAO estimates women are about 43% of the agricultural labour force in developing countries. What design check matters most?
opts: Whether the app can export records in the format the company's auditors prefer
Whether the app's interface follows the latest smartphone design conventions
Whether the app records yields per plot to the nearest kilogram for each crop
Whether women outgrowers can access the phones, data and training to use the app
quiz.x: Design decides who benefits; women often have less access to phones, data and training. Auditor exports matter for the company but do not determine whether a large share of growers is left out.

facts.t: Approximate share of the agricultural labour force in developing countries that is women.
facts.more: FAO's State of Food and Agriculture 2010–11 put the figure at about 43%. Women often have less access to phones, credit and training — so tool design decides who benefits.

facts.t: Share of food lost after harvest and before reaching retail, globally.
facts.more: FAO estimated about 14% of food is lost between harvest and retail. Post-harvest is a value-chain stage where record-keeping, storage advice and price information pay off.

facts.t: Value chain stages where AI can contribute: inputs to finance and risk.
facts.more: Inputs, production, post-harvest, processing, marketing, finance and risk. Mapping your stage first stops you buying a drone when your real problem is selling price.

facts.t: Year M-Pesa mobile money launched in Kenya.
facts.more: Mobile money showed that phone-based services can reach rural people at scale. Most valuable farm AI follows the same path: information delivered through the phone, not robots.

modules.d: Using AI for pest, disease and agronomic advice — accurately, safely and locally.
modules.body:
Diagnosis is a process, not a photo

Image-recognition apps can identify some pests and diseases from a phone photo. A well-known example is PlantVillage Nuru, developed by Penn State University's PlantVillage with partners including FAO and CGIAR centres, which works offline on smartphones and was trained to recognise cassava diseases and fall armyworm damage. Such tools are useful — but diagnosis is more than a photo. Agronomists combine the visual symptom with the crop's history, weather, field distribution of symptoms, soil and management practices.

Taking photos AI can use

  • Photograph in natural daylight, without strong shadows or glare.
  • Fill the frame with the affected part — leaf, stem, fruit or pod — in focus.
  • Take several images: close-up, whole plant and the field pattern.
  • Include both sides of leaves where relevant.
  • Note when symptoms started and how fast they are spreading.

Common problems in Cameroonian farming

Farmers frequently face cocoa black pod (caused by Phytophthora species, especially in humid conditions), cassava mosaic disease (a viral disease spread by whiteflies and infected cuttings), fall armyworm on maize (an invasive pest that spread across Africa from 2016), coffee leaf rust and berry diseases, banana and plantain diseases, and many vegetable pests. Some look alike; nutrient deficiencies and water stress can mimic disease. This is why AI suggestions must be checked.

Integrated Pest Management (IPM). Good advice — from AI or people — should follow IPM principles: prevention (resistant varieties, clean planting material, crop rotation, field hygiene), monitoring and thresholds (act when pest levels justify it), biological and cultural controls first, and chemical control only when needed, using registered products correctly with protective equipment. AI that jumps straight to "spray this chemical" is giving poor advice.

Asking AI good agronomic questions

General AI assistants can explain practices, suggest possible causes and outline management options when given context. A strong question includes: crop and variety, location and altitude, season and recent weather, symptoms and how they are distributed, field history, what has already been tried, and the farmer's resources. Then ask for possible causes ranked by likelihood, the observations that would distinguish them, prevention and management options following IPM, and what must be confirmed with an extension officer.

Soil and fertility

Fertiliser recommendations depend on soil tests, crop needs and local conditions. AI can explain soil test results and nutrient roles, but generic fertiliser rates can waste money or damage soils. Use soil testing services and local recommendations; ask AI to help interpret and plan within them.

Livestock

AI can help with record-keeping, feeding plans, vaccination schedules and understanding symptoms. Animal disease diagnosis and treatment, especially of notifiable diseases, require veterinarians; misuse of antibiotics drives resistance that threatens both animal and human health.

Extension workers and AI together

The strongest model combines AI with people: extension workers and lead farmers using AI tools to diagnose and advise more farmers more quickly, verifying uncertain cases, and feeding local observations back. Farmers trust advice demonstrated in their community.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my field agronomy assistant following Integrated Pest Management. I will describe my crop, variety, location, season, weather, symptoms, field pattern and history, and may upload photos. List possible causes ranked by likelihood, the observations that would distinguish them, prevention and management options starting with non-chemical methods, and exactly what I should confirm with an extension officer or veterinarian. Do not recommend specific pesticide doses.

📚 Glossary

  • PlantVillage Nuru: offline AI app for diagnosing crop diseases, developed by Penn State with partners
  • IPM: Integrated Pest Management — prevention, monitoring, thresholds, controls
  • Action threshold: pest level at which control is justified
  • Notifiable disease: animal disease that must be reported to authorities
  • Antimicrobial resistance: bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics through misuse

📖 References

  • PlantVillage (Penn State University) — Nuru app documentation.
  • FAO — Fall armyworm management guidance; Integrated Pest Management resources.
  • CABI — Plantwise Knowledge Bank.
  • IRAD Cameroon — crop protection recommendations.

quiz.q: A farmer near Bertoua photographs yellowing cassava leaves at noon in harsh sun, one blurry close-up, and an app returns 'cassava mosaic disease, 92%'. What should an agronomist advise?
opts: Treat for both mosaic and nutrient deficiency at once, since the two conditions can look alike
Retake several daylight photos (leaf, plant, field pattern) and note when symptoms began
Accept the result, since 92% confidence is high, and start uprooting the affected plants this week
Send the same photo to a second app and act on the diagnosis if both apps return a matching result
quiz.x: A good diagnosis needs proper photos plus history and field pattern. A second app on the same poor photo inherits the same weak evidence.

quiz.q: Maize in Garoua shows ragged holes and sawdust-like frass in the whorls. A chatbot immediately suggests a broad-spectrum insecticide. Under IPM, what should come first?
opts: Replant the whole field with a different crop to break the pest cycle before the damage spreads
Spray the recommended insecticide at once, because fall armyworm spreads fast across maize fields
Scout the field to estimate how many plants are infested and compare it with an action threshold
Apply wood ash to every plant as an organic option, then spray chemicals if damage still increases
quiz.x: IPM uses monitoring and thresholds before control. Wood ash is a cultural measure but applying it everywhere without scouting skips the monitoring step IPM requires.

quiz.q: A cassava farmer in the Centre region asks an AI how to stop mosaic disease, which reappears every season even after she removes sick plants. Which advice best targets the cause?
opts: Spray insecticide on whiteflies each month, since they are the main vector of the virus
Plant clean cuttings of resistant varieties, since the virus travels in planting material
Remove sick plants earlier in the season, before the first visible leaf symptoms spread
Apply extra fertiliser so plants grow strong enough to overcome the mosaic virus infection
quiz.x: Cassava mosaic spreads by whiteflies and infected cuttings; reusing infected cuttings keeps reintroducing it. Whitefly control is the runner-up but cannot fix a virus already present in the planting material.

quiz.q: A cocoa grower in the South West writes to an AI: 'My pods are rotting, what do I spray?' Which revision of the question would produce the most useful answer?
opts: Add a photo of one rotting pod and ask the AI to name the exact fungicide and dose to apply today
Ask the AI to respond as an expert plant pathologist so its answer carries more authority
Ask the AI to list every cocoa disease in Cameroon with a description of each one for comparison
Add variety, location, rain, pod symptoms and spread, past treatments; ask for ranked causes
quiz.x: Good agronomic questions give context and ask for ranked causes, distinguishing observations and IPM options. A role prompt changes tone, not the missing evidence.

quiz.q: A farmer in Foumbot wants to cut fertiliser costs on potatoes. An AI gives a generic NPK rate from a European guide. What is the soundest approach?
opts: Ask the AI to adjust the European rate for tropical soils and apply the revised figure directly
Halve last season's fertiliser rate and watch yields to see whether the crop really needed it
Get a soil test and local recommendation, then use AI to interpret results and plan within them
Apply the European rate, since potato nutrient needs are similar across most growing regions
quiz.x: Fertiliser rates depend on soil tests and local conditions. An AI-adjusted rate looks tailored but is still a guess without soil data.

quiz.q: Several pigs on a farm near Yaoundé have high fever and skin blotches; neighbours report deaths. The owner asks an AI which antibiotic to give. What is the right response?
opts: Call a vet urgently: it may be a notifiable disease, and antibiotics need a vet's decision
Isolate the sick pigs and follow the AI's suggested antibiotic course while the others are watched
Give a broad-spectrum antibiotic now to save the herd, then consult a vet if pigs do not improve
Ask the AI for a vaccination schedule, then vaccinate the healthy pigs to protect the rest of the herd
quiz.x: Animal disease diagnosis and treatment, especially of notifiable diseases, need a vet; antibiotic misuse drives resistance. Isolation is sensible but still pairs it with unprescribed antibiotics.

quiz.q: An extension programme in Ghana and Cameroon gives lead farmers PlantVillage Nuru on smartphones. A lead farmer finds an unfamiliar leaf spot on cowpea. What should she do?
opts: Rely on the app, because it runs offline and was developed with FAO and CGIAR partners for African crops
Treat the result as a hint and refer it to extension staff; cowpea may be outside its training
Photograph it under better light and accept the app's answer if confidence rises above about 80 percent
Advise the farmer to remove all spotted plants so any disease cannot spread while waiting for answers
quiz.x: Nuru was trained mainly on cassava diseases and fall armyworm; on other crops it can be confidently wrong. Better photos help, but higher confidence does not fix missing training data.

quiz.q: Leaves on a smallholder's tomatoes in Buea are yellowing between veins after three weeks of heavy rain. An app says 'early blight'. Why should the agronomist hesitate?
opts: Image apps cannot recognise tomato diseases, so any result from them on tomatoes is unreliable
Early blight does not occur in wet weather, so the diagnosis can be ruled out from the rain alone
The app should have been used before the rain, as photos taken after rainfall are rejected
Nutrient deficiency from leaching can mimic disease; the field pattern and history need checking
quiz.x: Nutrient deficiencies and water stress can mimic disease, so context matters. Saying apps cannot recognise tomato diseases overstates the limit; the issue is confirming this case.

quiz.q: A cooperative in Kenya and one in Cameroon both want AI-backed advisory. Which delivery model does the module present as strongest?
opts: Farmers query AI directly, with extension workers reserved for an annual training at the cooperative
A central call centre staffed by agronomists answers by phone, using AI to log calls for reports
Extension staff and lead farmers use AI to advise faster, verify hard cases, feed back data
AI advice is sent by SMS to all members, and demonstration plots are dropped to save on budget
quiz.x: Combining AI with people who verify and demonstrate builds trust and accuracy. A call centre uses experts but uses AI just for logging and loses local demonstration.

quiz.q: Fall armyworm was first reported in Africa in 2016. A farmer in Ngaoundéré uses a maize guide written in 2012. Why might AI-assisted advice still need checking against current sources?
opts: Pest pressures change; advice from before the pest arrived may miss today's control options
The guide was written for drier zones, and Ngaoundéré's climate has become fully humid
AI tools cannot read documents older than about ten years and will skip the 2012 material
Maize varieties grown in 2012 have since been withdrawn, so the guide's spacing is now illegal
quiz.x: Fall armyworm spread after 2016, so older guidance and AI trained on it can be out of date. The other options invent constraints the module does not support.

facts.t: Year fall armyworm was first reported in Africa.
facts.more: First detected in West and Central Africa in 2016, it spread across most of sub-Saharan Africa within about two years — a reason maize advice must stay current.

facts.t: Main insect vector of cassava mosaic disease — alongside infected cuttings.
facts.more: Because the virus also travels in planting material, clean cuttings and resistant varieties are prevention steps no spray can replace.

facts.t: Deaths directly attributable to bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019.
facts.more: Antibiotic misuse in people and animals drives resistance. That is why AI must never prescribe livestock antibiotics — vets decide.

facts.t: PlantVillage Nuru runs on a smartphone without a data connection.
facts.more: Developed by Penn State's PlantVillage with FAO and CGIAR partners, trained on cassava diseases and fall armyworm. Offline matters where signal is weak — but it only knows what it was trained on.

labs.title: Climb the IPM ladder
labs.intro: A maize farmer near Garoua sees leaf damage. Put the IPM-consistent response in order.
steps: Use clean seed, resistant varieties and rotation before the season
Scout the field regularly and record damage levels
Compare counts with the action threshold
Apply cultural or biological controls first
Use a registered product correctly, with PPE, only if still justified
Record results and share them with the extension officer
labs.tip: Prevention → monitoring → threshold → non-chemical → chemical last → learn. AI that starts at 'spray' skips four rungs.

labs.title: Spot the problems in this AI field advice
labs.intro: A farmer pasted one blurry photo of a cocoa pod into a chatbot. Tap every phrase that should not be acted on.
segments: Thanks for the photo.
This is 100% cocoa black pod, no other cause is possible.
One blurry photo cannot rule out other causes; false certainty is a red flag.
Black pod is caused by Phytophthora and spreads in humid weather,
so remove and bury infected pods to reduce spores.
Spray 5 kg per litre of any copper product you find at the market
Invented dose and unregistered product choice — pesticide advice must follow local registration and labels.
every two days until the rains stop.
Excessive, unsafe frequency with no threshold — contradicts IPM.
Also prune shade to improve air flow around the trees.
No need to wear gloves; copper is natural.
Dangerous: 'natural' does not mean safe — PPE is always required.
Ask your extension officer to confirm.
labs.tip: Check certainty, product, dose, frequency and safety. Cultural controls are usually sound; chemical specifics need local authority.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the cassava field visit
plaibox.intro: You are a lead farmer in Bertoua helping a neighbour whose cassava leaves look mottled and twisted. Make each call.
plaibox.win: Strong diagnosis practice — good evidence, ranked causes, prevention before chemicals, and verification.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the photo protocol and IPM: evidence first, prevention over sprays, and confirm uncertain cases with extension.

steps.s: Your neighbour wants to send one quick photo to an AI app right now, at noon in harsh sun.
o: Send it now; the app adjusts for poor lighting
Glare and a single angle cause false-confident diagnoses.
Take close-up, whole-plant and field shots in soft light
Right — several angles in good light give the model and the officer real evidence.
Skip photos and describe the leaves to the agent by phone
Descriptions help, but images of the field pattern are valuable evidence.

steps.s: The app says 'cassava mosaic disease, 71% confidence'. What next?
o: Treat 71% as confirmed and act before it spreads
A probability is not a diagnosis; similar symptoms have other causes.
Note whiteflies, spread and cutting source to test it
Correct — distinguishing observations confirm or rule out the suggestion.
Ignore the app because 71% is too low to trust at all
Discarding it wastes a useful lead; test it with observations instead.

steps.s: It looks like mosaic. A trader offers an insecticide 'that cures mosaic'.
o: Buy it, since whiteflies are what spread the virus
No spray cures a virus in infected plants; this wastes money and risks health.
Rogue infected plants; replant with clean resistant cuttings
Prevention and clean planting material are the core IPM response for a viral disease.
Spray only the worst corner as a trial to see the effect
Less harm, but it still targets the wrong problem.

steps.s: Other farms in the village show the same symptoms.
o: Report to the extension officer with field notes
Feeding local observations back helps the whole area and gets authoritative advice.
Post the AI diagnosis in the WhatsApp group as fact
Unverified advice spreads quickly and can cause wrong action across many farms.
Wait two weeks to see if it spreads to other plots
Monitoring matters, but delaying a report lets an outbreak grow.

modules.d: Advisory apps, weather and satellite services, market platforms and farm management tools — evaluated for real farms.
modules.body:
Evaluate by farmer reality

Agricultural technology products appear and disappear quickly, and many pilots never scale. Evaluate tools by whether they work for your farmers' devices, languages, connectivity, crops and budgets — and verify current availability, costs and data terms directly with providers.

Main categories

  • Diagnosis and advisory apps: image-based pest and disease identification (for example PlantVillage Nuru) and agronomic advice databases (for example CABI's Plantwise resources).
  • General AI assistants: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others — useful for explanations, planning and business documents when given local context; not authoritative on local regulations or registered products.
  • Weather and climate services: forecasts and seasonal outlooks from national meteorological services and international providers, sometimes delivered by SMS or radio.
  • Satellite and remote sensing: free imagery such as Sentinel-2 (from the European Copernicus programme) and Landsat enables vegetation monitoring; platforms analyse crop health, water stress and yield trends — more relevant to cooperatives, agribusinesses and programmes than to individual smallholders.
  • Market information and trading platforms: price information, buyer–seller matching, and digital marketplaces.
  • Digital financial services: mobile money, digital credit and index insurance, often linked to farm records.
  • Farm and cooperative management: record-keeping, member registration, collection and payment tracking, traceability for export certification (important for cocoa and coffee).
  • Messaging channels: WhatsApp groups, SMS, voice services (IVR) and community radio — often the most effective delivery channel for advice.
Traceability is becoming a market requirement. Major buyers and regulations — such as the European Union's deforestation regulation affecting commodities including cocoa and coffee — increasingly require proof of where and how crops were produced, sometimes including farm geolocation. Cooperatives that build reliable digital records and mapping gain market access; those that do not may lose buyers. Check the current requirements and timelines for your markets.

Evaluation criteria

  1. Local accuracy: tested on your crops, varieties, pests and conditions.
  2. Access: works on basic phones or offline; affordable data use; voice and local languages.
  3. Trust and support: local partners, extension integration, training and help.
  4. Data ownership and privacy: who owns farmers' data, how it is used and shared, and whether farmers consent.
  5. Cost and business model: who pays, sustainability after donor funding ends.
  6. Interoperability: data exports, integration with cooperative and buyer systems.
  7. Evidence of impact: yields, incomes, losses or costs improved in comparable settings.

Farmer data rights

Farm data — location, production, sales, finances — has value to buyers, lenders, insurers and platforms. Farmers and cooperatives should understand what data is collected, who can use it, and what they receive in return. Cooperatives can negotiate collectively for fair data terms.

Choosing a starting set

A cooperative might start with: a record-keeping and member management tool, a messaging channel for advice and prices, access to a diagnosis app for lead farmers, a general AI assistant for business documents, and partnerships with weather and extension services. Expand based on proven value.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my agri-technology advisor. Ask me whether I am a farmer, cooperative, agribusiness or programme, my crops, members' phones and languages, and my market requirements (including export traceability). Recommend tool categories, a scoring sheet using the seven criteria, a starting set, and the data-rights questions I should ask providers.

📚 Glossary

  • Remote sensing: observing crops from satellites or drones
  • Sentinel-2: free satellite imagery from the EU Copernicus programme
  • Traceability: ability to trace a product to its origin and production practices
  • IVR: interactive voice response — phone-based voice menus
  • Farmer data rights: farmers' control over and benefit from data about their farms

📖 References

  • CABI — Plantwise Knowledge Bank.
  • European Space Agency — Copernicus Sentinel-2.
  • European Union — Regulation on deforestation-free products (check current application dates).
  • GODAN / CTA — farmer data rights resources.

quiz.q: A cooperative in Ayos exports cocoa to Europe. Its buyer warns that proof of farm location will be needed under the EU deforestation regulation. What should the cooperative prioritise?
opts: Map members' farms with geolocation and keep reliable digital production and sales records too
Ask the buyer to handle compliance since the regulation applies to EU operators, not farmers
Buy a premium satellite platform to measure canopy health on every member's farm each week
Switch to selling cocoa within the region, since EU rules make European buyers unprofitable
quiz.x: EUDR requires proof of where crops were produced, often geolocation; reliable records keep market access. Satellite monitoring is related but does not itself produce the plot-level traceability buyers ask for.

quiz.q: Under the EUDR, cocoa sold into the EU must come from land not deforested after a cut-off date. A plot was cleared from forest in mid-2021. What is the likely consequence?
opts: Its cocoa is compliant once the farmer has held the plot for at least three full seasons
Its cocoa is compliant, as the cut-off date applies to clearing after 31 December 2022
It is not EU-compliant, since the clearing came after the 31 December 2020 cut-off
Its cocoa is compliant if the cooperative replants shade trees on the plot within a year
quiz.x: The cut-off date is 31 December 2020, so mid-2021 clearing fails. Replanting shade trees is good practice but does not change the deforestation date.

quiz.q: An NGO programme in Cameroon wants to monitor 5,000 hectares of cocoa landscapes, while a smallholder wants to see disease on her single 0.5 ha plot. How suitable is free Sentinel-2 imagery?
opts: Useful for neither, because free satellite imagery is too old to support any decisions
Suits the landscape programme; at 10 m pixels it is too coarse to see her plants
Useful for both, since 10 m resolution can resolve individual cocoa trees on small plots
Useful for the smallholder, as free imagery is designed for individual farm diagnosis
quiz.x: Sentinel-2's 10 m pixels suit landscape monitoring but cannot show individual plants. Saying it helps both overstates resolution.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian agtech start-up offers a free farm-records app to a 900-member coffee cooperative. The terms let the company sell farm data to lenders and buyers. What should the board do?
opts: Let each member read the terms and decide alone whether their own data can be sold
Decline all digital tools, keeping paper records so that farm data cannot be misused
Accept, since the app is free and data sharing may help members get loans from lenders
Negotiate jointly on what is shared, with whom, with member consent and fair benefits
quiz.x: Farm data has value; cooperatives can negotiate fair terms collectively. Individual choice respects consent but leaves members weak in bargaining with the company.

quiz.q: Comparing two pest-advice apps for maize in Northern Cameroon: App A has strong lab accuracy abroad but needs 4G; App B works offline on basic Android, tested in Nigeria and Chad. Which criteria favour B?
opts: Interoperability and cost: it exports data to buyers and has a clear long-term model
Evidence of impact: it has proven yield gains in randomised trials across Cameroon
Reach and fit: runs without data coverage and was validated near similar Sahel zones
Data ownership and support: it stores data locally and has local partner training
quiz.x: Offline use and testing in neighbouring Sahel conditions match the access and local-accuracy criteria. The other options claim facts not given in the scenario.

quiz.q: A donor-funded diagnosis app has served a district in Cameroon free for two years; funding ends in six months. What evaluation criterion should a cooperative have checked from the start?
opts: Cost and business model: who pays and whether the service survives after donor money
Access: whether the app works on basic phones and in the local languages of members
Local accuracy: whether it was tested on the district's main crops and common pests
Interoperability: whether its data exports fit the cooperative's buyer reporting systems
quiz.x: Sustainability after donor funding is the cost and business model criterion. Local accuracy matters too, but an accurate tool that shuts down still leaves members stranded.

quiz.q: A US-based coffee importer asks a Cameroonian cooperative to prove its beans did not come from recently cleared forest. Which free data source helps compare today's cover with the past?
opts: A general AI assistant asked to describe the forest history of each member's village
Landsat imagery, whose archive back to 1972 allows before-and-after cover comparison
WhatsApp group photos of farms, shared by members as visual evidence for the buyer
Daily weather forecasts from the national meteorological service for the growing areas
quiz.x: Landsat's long archive allows comparison of past and present cover, which deforestation checks rely on. Member photos show current conditions but not past cover.

quiz.q: A cooperative manager in Bafia plans to use ChatGPT to answer members' questions on which pesticides are currently approved in Cameroon. What is the main concern?
opts: General assistants charge per question, making them too costly for a cooperative budget
General assistants are banned for agricultural use in Cameroon under current regulations
General assistants cannot work in French, which members need for written agronomic advice
General assistants are not authoritative on local registration; lists must come from authorities
quiz.x: General AI is useful for explanations and documents but not authoritative on local regulations or registered products. The other options are false claims.

quiz.q: A new 300-member cocoa cooperative in the Littoral asks where to start with digital tools. Which starter set best matches the module's advice?
opts: A smartphone for every member, a diagnosis app for all, and a paid market-trading platform licence
A satellite monitoring platform, drones for spraying, a traceability system and a custom AI model built
A single all-in-one platform from one vendor covering advice, finance, insurance and traceability
Member records, WhatsApp/SMS channel, diagnosis app for lead farmers, AI assistant for business documents
quiz.x: The module suggests a modest starter set, then expanding on proven value. An all-in-one platform is tempting but risks lock-in and weak interoperability before value is proven.

quiz.q: Evaluating an index insurance and digital credit app for maize farmers in Cameroon, which question best tests 'evidence of impact'?
opts: Does the app use the latest machine-learning models for predicting rainfall risk?
How many downloads has the app reached across Africa since it launched publicly?
Did farmers in similar settings gain on incomes, yields or losses after using it?
How many international awards and grants has the provider received in recent years?
quiz.x: Evidence of impact means improvements in yields, incomes, losses or costs in comparable settings. Downloads show reach, not results.

facts.t: Finest ground resolution of free Sentinel-2 imagery.
facts.more: Good for field- and landscape-scale monitoring by cooperatives and programmes; too coarse to see individual plants on a small plot.

facts.t: Year the first Landsat satellite launched — the longest Earth-observation record.
facts.more: Decades of free imagery let analysts compare today's vegetation and forest cover with the past, which is exactly what deforestation checks rely on.

facts.t: Deforestation cut-off date in the EU deforestation regulation (EUDR).
facts.more: Cocoa and coffee sold into the EU must come from land not deforested after this date, proven with geolocation. Check current application timelines — they have been postponed before.

facts.t: Commodities covered by the EUDR.
facts.more: Cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood. For Cameroon, cocoa, coffee, rubber, palm oil and timber are all affected — farm mapping is now a market requirement.

o: Sign now; free mapping tools for co-ops are rare
Free often means farmers' data is the payment; members never consented.

Right — cooperatives can bargain for consent, limits and benefit-sharing.

steps.s: Terms are improved. How do you start?

Scaling before testing accuracy and phone fit risks bad data at scale.
Pilot with 20 farms, compare with GPS checks
A small pilot measures accuracy and usability before rollout.
Let each farmer decide alone whether to use it

steps.s: Pilot maps are good, but older women members struggle with the app.
o: Proceed anyway; younger members can carry the cooperative
Excluding women widens inequality and leaves their plots untraceable.
Have trained youth map plots with them, explaining consent
Intermediaries keep inclusion and consent while getting the data right.
Pause the whole programme until the app adds voice input
Inclusive intent, but delays market access for everyone.

o: Check data export rights and compare options now
Interoperability and exit plans protect you from lock-in.
Accept — the data is already in their system
Pragmatic, but you may be paying for lock-in rather than value.
Stop paying and lose access to the maps
Without an export, years of traceability data could vanish.

modules.d: Records, costs, margins, markets and finance — with AI as the farmer's business assistant.
modules.body:
From farming to agribusiness

Many farmers work extremely hard yet do not know which crop, plot or season actually makes money. Treating the farm as a business — keeping records, knowing costs, planning sales and accessing finance — is often the most powerful step toward higher incomes. AI makes these business tasks easier for people without formal business training.

Records: the foundation

Records should cover inputs bought (seed, fertiliser, chemicals, labour), quantities used, production per plot, sales (quantity, price, buyer, date), and loans and repayments. They can be kept in a notebook, a spreadsheet or an app. AI can help design a simple record template, turn voice notes or photos of receipts into tables, and summarise records into reports.

Costs and gross margin

The gross margin of an enterprise (for example one hectare of maize) is revenue minus variable costs — seed, fertiliser, chemicals, hired labour, transport and bags. Comparing gross margins per hectare, per day of labour or per franc invested shows which enterprises deserve more resources. The cost of production per kilogram (total costs ÷ kilograms produced) tells a farmer the minimum price needed to avoid a loss.

Worked example. A farmer produces 2,500 kg of maize on one hectare and sells at 180 FCFA/kg: revenue 450,000 FCFA. Variable costs: seed 40,000; fertiliser 120,000; hired labour 90,000; transport and bags 35,000 — total 285,000 FCFA. Gross margin = 165,000 FCFA per hectare. Cost of production = 285,000 ÷ 2,500 = 114 FCFA/kg. Selling below 114 FCFA/kg would not cover variable costs. Ask AI to build these calculations as spreadsheet formulas so they update automatically.

Market and price strategy

Prices often fall at harvest and rise later. Options include improved storage to sell later (weighing storage costs and losses), collective selling through cooperatives to negotiate better prices, contracts with buyers, quality grading for premium prices, and value addition (drying, processing, packaging). AI can summarise market price information, compare scenarios, draft buyer communications and help prepare simple contracts — reviewed carefully.

Value addition and new products

Processing cassava into gari or flour, plantain into chips, cocoa into higher-grade beans, or fruit into juice can increase income — but also adds costs, food safety requirements and marketing work. AI can help research product ideas, calculate costs, draft labels within regulations, and plan marketing; food safety and regulatory requirements must be verified with authorities.

Accessing finance

Lenders and microfinance institutions want to see records, a business plan, cash flow projections and evidence of repayment ability. AI can help farmers and cooperatives draft a clear business plan, prepare cash flow forecasts showing when money comes in and goes out across the season, and explain loan terms (interest rates, repayment schedules, total cost). Never sign a loan without understanding the total repayment and risks.

Cooperatives as businesses

Cooperatives aggregate members' produce, negotiate prices, provide inputs and services, and access markets individuals cannot. Good governance — transparent accounts, fair payment, elected leadership and member participation — determines whether they succeed. AI can help cooperatives with member records, reports, minutes, financial summaries and communication — supporting transparency, which builds member trust.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my farm business assistant. I will give you my crops, area, yields, prices and costs. Build spreadsheet formulas for revenue, variable costs, gross margin per hectare and cost of production per kilogram for each enterprise, compare them, and identify which enterprise deserves more investment. Then help me draft a simple seasonal cash flow forecast and a one-page business plan for a loan application, flagging assumptions I must verify.

📚 Glossary

  • Gross margin: revenue minus variable costs for an enterprise
  • Cost of production: total cost divided by quantity produced
  • Value addition: processing or improving products to increase value
  • Cash flow forecast: projection of money coming in and going out over time
  • Collective marketing: selling together through a group or cooperative

📖 References

  • FAO — Farm business management and gross margin analysis guides.
  • ILO — Cooperative development resources.
  • CGAP — Digital finance for smallholder farmers.
  • Cameroon Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MINADER) — programme information.

quiz.q: A maize farmer in Bafang produced 2,000 kg on one hectare and sold at 200 FCFA/kg. Variable costs were 260,000 FCFA. What is her gross margin per hectare?
opts: 140,000 FCFA, from revenue of 400,000 minus the 260,000
260,000 FCFA, from total variable costs paid in cash
400,000 FCFA, as the revenue covered all of her costs
130,000 FCFA, from cost of production times 1,000 kg
quiz.x: 2,000 x 200 = 400,000 revenue; minus 260,000 = 140,000 FCFA. 130,000 confuses cost per kg (130 FCFA) with margin.

quiz.q: Using the same figures (2,000 kg, variable costs 260,000 FCFA), a trader offers 125 FCFA/kg at harvest. What should the farmer understand?
opts: 125 equals her break-even price, so she neither gains nor loses on variable costs at that rate
125 is below her 130 FCFA/kg cost of production, so the sale would not cover her variable costs
125 is above her 120 FCFA/kg cost of production, so the sale leaves a small positive margin
125 is fine because gross margin is positive at any price above half the market price of 200
quiz.x: Cost of production = 260,000 / 2,000 = 130 FCFA/kg; selling at 125 loses money. The 120 figure is a miscalculation.

quiz.q: A farmer in Bamenda compares 1 ha maize (gross margin 165,000 FCFA, 60 labour days) and 0.25 ha tomatoes (gross margin 150,000 FCFA, 75 labour days). Labour is her scarcest resource. Which is better per labour day?
opts: Maize: it earns a higher total margin, which is the measure that matters most here
Maize: about 2,750 FCFA per labour day versus 2,000 FCFA per day for tomatoes
Tomatoes: they earn 600,000 FCFA per hectare, so they beat maize on all measures
Tomatoes: about 2,000 FCFA per day versus 1,650 FCFA per day for maize
quiz.x: 165,000/60 = 2,750 and 150,000/75 = 2,000 per day. Tomatoes win per hectare, a defensible runner-up, but labour is the constraint here.

quiz.q: Maize sells at 150 FCFA/kg at harvest and is expected near 210 FCFA/kg four months later. Storage bags and treatment cost 10 FCFA/kg and about 10% of grain may be lost. Is storing likely worth it?
opts: No: a 10% loss plus storage costs wipes out the 60 FCFA price rise over the four months
Yes: the gain is the full 60 FCFA per kg, since storage costs are already counted as sunk
No: storage makes sense once the expected later price is at least double the harvest price
Yes: 90% of 210 is 189, minus 10 storage, gives about 179 FCFA per kg stored versus 150 now
quiz.x: 0.9 x 210 = 189; minus 10 = 179 per kg stored, above 150. The 'full 60 FCFA' answer ignores losses and storage costs.

quiz.q: A microfinance institution in Douala asks a cassava cooperative for evidence it can repay a 5 million FCFA input loan. Which package is strongest?
opts: Records of past production and sales, a business plan and a season cash flow forecast
A list of members and their land sizes, with a projection of yields at maximum output
A letter from the mayor confirming the cooperative is well known and respected locally
Photos of members' fields and a description of the cooperative's history and values
quiz.x: Lenders want records, a business plan, cash flow projections and evidence of repayment ability. Member and land lists are useful but optimistic yields do not show repayment capacity.

quiz.q: A farmer is offered a 500,000 FCFA loan at 3% per month flat for 6 months by one lender and 24% per year flat for 6 months by another. Which is cheaper in total interest?
opts: The 3% per month loan: 90,000 FCFA interest versus 120,000 FCFA at 24% per year
They cost the same, since 3% per month and 24% per year are equivalent annual rates
The 24% per year loan: 60,000 FCFA interest versus 90,000 FCFA at 3% per month flat
The 3% per month loan: 15,000 FCFA interest versus 60,000 FCFA at 24% per year

quiz.q: A women's group in Mbouda wants to turn cassava into packaged gari for supermarkets in Yaoundé. How should they use AI in planning?
opts: Ask AI to confirm which food-safety approvals they need, and treat its answer as the official list
Let AI estimate the selling price from online data, then scale up production to supermarket volumes
Skip costing for now and use AI mainly to design an attractive label and a social media campaign
Research the market, cost the process, draft labels, then check food-safety rules with authorities
quiz.x: AI can research, cost and draft, but food safety and regulatory requirements must be verified with authorities. Asking AI for the approvals list treats it as authoritative when it is not.

quiz.q: A coffee cooperative in the West region has falling member trust after disputes over payments. Which AI use best supports good governance?
opts: Produce clear monthly summaries of collections, payments and accounts shared with all members
Automate payment decisions with an AI model so that leaders no longer handle member payments
Build a members' chatbot that answers questions about the cooperative's history and its values
Draft persuasive messages from leaders explaining why members should trust the current board
quiz.x: Transparency in accounts and payments builds trust, consistent with ICA principles. Persuasive messaging addresses perception, not the underlying lack of transparency.

quiz.q: A tomato grower in Foumbot sells everything at harvest when prices fall. Which option best addresses this through collective action?
opts: Asking AI each morning for the best market price and driving to that market alone
Selling through the cooperative as a group, with contracts agreed with bulk buyers
Storing fresh tomatoes at home for two months until prices recover in the dry season
Planting twice the area next season so that the larger volume offsets the low prices
quiz.x: Collective selling and contracts improve bargaining power. Daily price checks help but a lone farmer still lacks volume and bargaining power, and fresh tomatoes store poorly.

quiz.q: A farmer in a Bamenda njangi has repaid every rotation for six years and now seeks a first bank loan. How might AI help most?
opts: Calculate the largest loan she could request based on the total value of her land holdings
Write a loan application that projects record yields to make repayment look more certain
Turn her njangi history and records into a cash flow and business plan for the lender
Draft a letter asking the bank to waive its documentation requirements for a loyal saver
quiz.x: Njangi repayment history and records are evidence of discipline a lender may value; AI can structure them into a plan. Inflated projections undermine credibility.

facts.t: Gross margin per hectare in the module's maize example.
facts.more: 2,500 kg × 180 FCFA = 450,000 revenue, minus 285,000 variable costs. Gross margin lets you compare maize against cassava or tomatoes on the same land.

facts.t: Cost of production in the same example — the floor price.
facts.more: 285,000 ÷ 2,500 kg. Selling below this loses money on variable costs alone; any storage strategy must beat it plus storage losses.

facts.t: ICA cooperative principles, including democratic member control.
facts.more: The International Co-operative Alliance's seven principles include member economic participation and education. Transparent AI-assisted reports support them.

facts.t: Rotating savings groups common across Cameroon.
facts.more: Also called tontines. They are a familiar base for collective saving and, for many farmers, the first record of repayment discipline a lender might value.

modules.d: Weather, climate adaptation, insurance and diversification — planning for uncertainty.
modules.body:
Farming in a changing climate

Farmers across Central and West Africa report shifting rainy seasons, longer dry spells, heavier rains, rising temperatures and new pest pressures. These changes increase risk for every planting decision. Climate-smart agriculture helps farmers manage this uncertainty — and AI can make weather and climate information more usable.

Climate-smart agriculture

FAO describes climate-smart agriculture (CSA) through three pillars: sustainably increasing productivity and incomes, adapting and building resilience to climate change, and reducing or removing greenhouse gas emissions where possible. Practices include drought-tolerant and early-maturing varieties, soil conservation and mulching, agroforestry (important for cocoa and coffee), water harvesting and efficient irrigation, crop diversification, integrated crop–livestock systems and reduced post-harvest losses.

Using weather and climate information

Different timescales support different decisions. Daily and weekly forecasts help decide when to spray, harvest or dry produce. Seasonal forecasts — probabilistic outlooks of whether rainfall is likely to be above, near or below normal — inform choices of variety, planting date and area. Long-term climate projections inform investments such as tree crops or irrigation. AI can translate forecasts into plain-language advice in local languages, and help farmers plan options under different scenarios.

Understanding probability. A seasonal forecast of "60% chance of below-normal rainfall" does not mean drought is certain. It means planning should prepare for drier conditions — for example favouring drought-tolerant varieties on part of the land — while keeping options for normal rains. AI can help explain probabilities and build "if–then" plans.

Risk management strategies

  • Diversification: several crops, varieties, livestock or off-farm income so one failure does not ruin the household.
  • Staggered planting to spread risk across rainfall patterns.
  • Savings and group funds: village savings and loan associations (such as njangi/tontines) provide buffers.
  • Insurance: index insurance pays out when an index — such as measured rainfall or satellite vegetation indices — crosses a threshold, rather than assessing each farm's loss. This lowers costs but creates basis risk: a farmer may suffer losses even when the index does not trigger, or vice versa.
  • Storage and post-harvest management to reduce losses and allow flexible selling.
  • Information and early warning: pest outbreaks, floods and droughts.

Agroforestry and climate

Shade trees in cocoa and coffee systems can moderate temperature, protect soils, diversify income (fruit, timber) and store carbon. They require good management to balance shade with productivity. AI can help farmers and cooperatives plan tree species and spacing using local recommendations.

Carbon and environmental markets — with caution

Some programmes offer payments for carbon storage or sustainable practices. These can create income, but contracts are often complex, payments uncertain and verification demanding. Farmers and cooperatives should seek independent advice and understand obligations before signing.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my climate-smart planning advisor. I will give you my crops, location, typical season and the latest seasonal forecast (with probabilities). Explain the forecast in plain language, build an if–then plan for drier, normal and wetter scenarios covering varieties, planting dates and area, and recommend risk management measures including diversification and insurance, noting the basis risk of any index insurance.

📚 Glossary

  • Climate-smart agriculture: productivity, adaptation and mitigation together
  • Seasonal forecast: probabilistic outlook of rainfall or temperature for a season
  • Index insurance: insurance paid when an index crosses a threshold
  • Basis risk: mismatch between an index payout and actual farm loss
  • Agroforestry: integrating trees with crops or livestock

📖 References

  • FAO — Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook.
  • IPCC — Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group II (Africa chapter).
  • CGIAR — Climate adaptation and index insurance research.
  • World Agroforestry (ICRAF) — cocoa and coffee agroforestry resources.

quiz.q: A seasonal outlook for Adamawa gives a 60% chance of below-normal rainfall. A maize farmer asks whether to plant only drought-tolerant varieties. What is the best advice?
opts: Plant drought-tolerant varieties across the whole farm, since drought is now the likely outcome
Delay all planting until the rains are established, then decide on varieties for the season
Set the outlook aside and plant as usual, since a 40% chance of normal rain remains quite high
Plant drought-tolerant, early varieties on part of the land and keep options for normal rains
quiz.x: 60% is not certain; hedging prepares for dry conditions while keeping options. Planting all drought-tolerant varieties bets everything on one scenario.

quiz.q: A cocoa farmer in the Centre region wants to decide, for the coming week, when to spray against black pod and when to dry beans. Which information timescale fits?
opts: Daily and weekly forecasts covering the next several days of local weather
Seasonal outlooks giving rainfall probabilities for the next three months
Historical averages of rainfall for the same week over the past ten years
Long-term climate projections for the region over the coming decades
quiz.x: Short-range forecasts suit spraying and drying decisions. Historical averages give context but not this week's weather.

quiz.q: A maize farmer in Garoua holds rainfall index insurance. A hailstorm destroys her crop, but the season's measured rainfall is normal, so there is no payout. What concept explains this?
opts: Moral hazard: farmers taking more risk because they know they are insured
Adverse selection: high-risk farmers buying insurance more than others
Basis risk: a mismatch between what was measured and what she lost
Premium risk: insurers raising prices after a bad season in the region
quiz.x: Index insurance pays on the index, not field loss; hail with normal rainfall is basis risk. The others are real insurance concepts but do not fit this case.

quiz.q: A carbon programme offers Cameroonian cocoa farmers payments for planting shade trees, under a 30-year contract with complex verification. What should a cooperative do first?
opts: Refuse, because carbon programmes in Africa have been shown not to pay farmers anything
Seek independent advice to understand obligations, verification and payment uncertainty
Ask an AI assistant to summarise the contract, then sign if the summary looks favourable
Sign quickly for all members, since early adopters usually get the best carbon prices
quiz.x: Carbon contracts are complex and uncertain; independent advice is the module's guidance. An AI summary is a useful step but not a substitute for independent review.

quiz.q: In FAO's climate-smart agriculture framework, a cocoa cooperative introduces shade trees. Which pillars does this practice touch?
opts: All three: fruit and timber income, a cooler microclimate and carbon stored in trees
Productivity and mitigation: more timber income and stored carbon, but no adaptation
Mitigation alone: shade trees store carbon but do not affect income or resilience
Adaptation alone: shade trees protect cocoa from heat but reduce cocoa productivity
quiz.x: Agroforestry touches all three pillars when managed to balance shade with productivity. The adaptation-only option ignores fruit and timber income and stored carbon.

quiz.q: A smallholder household in the North West grows only maize and depends on it for food and cash. Drought has hit twice in five years. Which risk strategy most reduces the chance of total ruin?
opts: Plant all maize earlier in the season so the crop matures before the dry spells arrive
Use AI weather forecasts to time planting so the maize avoids dry spells in each season
Buy index insurance for maize, so that a poor season of rainfall triggers a payout to them
Diversify into other crops, livestock or off-farm work so one failure is not total ruin
quiz.x: Diversification spreads risk across enterprises. Index insurance is a strong runner-up but has basis risk and still leaves the household dependent on one crop.

quiz.q: A cooperative in the Littoral wants to use AI to explain a seasonal forecast to members who speak Duala and Pidgin. Which approach fits the module?
opts: Post the forecast in French on the cooperative's notice board for members to consult
Have AI translate the outlook into plain-language voice messages with if-then options
Send the meteorological agency's full technical bulletin by SMS so nothing is simplified
Have AI convert the forecast into a single firm prediction so members are not confused
quiz.x: AI can translate forecasts into plain language and if-then plans in local languages. A single firm prediction misrepresents a probabilistic forecast.

quiz.q: A farmer in Kenya and one in Cameroon each face a 50% chance of a late rainy-season start. Which if-then plan is best?
opts: Plant early-maturing varieties on the whole farm regardless of when the rains begin
Wait for an AI forecast just before planting and follow whichever scenario it predicts
If rains start by week X, plant main varieties; if later, switch to early-maturing ones
Plant main varieties on the usual date, then replant if the seedlings fail to emerge
quiz.x: If-then plans set decision triggers in advance for different scenarios. Replanting after failure is a fallback that wastes seed and time.

quiz.q: A cooperative wants to protect members from losing maize stocks to pests and moisture after harvest. Which climate-risk strategy from the module fits?
opts: Staggered planting dates to spread harvest across several different rainfall patterns
Index insurance that pays out when satellite vegetation indices fall below a threshold
Better storage and post-harvest handling to cut losses and allow flexible selling
Long-term climate projections to decide which tree crops to invest in over a decade
quiz.x: Storage and post-harvest management reduce losses and allow flexible selling. Index insurance covers field yield risks, not storage losses.

quiz.q: A coffee farmer in Dschang has a 60% chance of above-normal rain this season. Which response best fits the probability?
opts: Assume heavy rain is certain and reduce the coffee area to limit potential disease losses
Wait until heavy rain arrives before taking any action to manage coffee disease risk
Set the outlook aside, since probabilities below 70% are not meaningful for farm decisions
Prepare for wetter conditions (drainage, disease scouting) while keeping normal plans
quiz.x: Probabilistic forecasts call for hedged preparation. Treating 60% as certain overreacts.

facts.t: FAO's climate-smart agriculture: productivity, adaptation, mitigation.
facts.more: Sustainably raise productivity and incomes, adapt and build resilience, and reduce emissions where possible. Agroforestry in cocoa touches all three.

facts.t: A 60% chance of below-normal rain still leaves a 40% chance it won't be.
facts.more: Seasonal forecasts are probabilities. Plan a hedge — e.g. drought-tolerant varieties on part of the land — rather than betting everything on one scenario.

facts.t: The gap between an index insurance payout and a farmer's real loss.
facts.more: Payouts follow measured rainfall or satellite indices, not field inspections. A hail-damaged farm can get nothing if the index stays normal — explain this before farmers buy.

facts.t: Daily/weekly forecasts, seasonal outlooks, long-term projections.
facts.more: Each fits a different decision: when to spray or dry, which variety and planting date, and whether to invest in trees or irrigation.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the dry-season outlook
plaibox.intro: You advise a maize and bean group near Bafoussam. The seasonal outlook gives 60% chance of below-normal rain.
plaibox.win: Good climate-smart reasoning: hedged against probability, explained basis risk and kept options open.
plaibox.lose: Revisit probability and basis risk: plan for scenarios, don't bet on one, and explain insurance limits honestly.

steps.s: Members ask: 'So there will be a drought?'
o: Yes, prepare for drought on all plots
Treats 60% as certainty and gives up yield if rains are normal.
Drier is more likely, so hedge part of the land
Correct reading of probability, with a balanced response.
Forecasts are often wrong; plant as usual
Ignores useful information that shifts the odds.

steps.s: How should the group adjust planting?
o: Early-maturing seed on about half, staggered dates
Diversifies across scenarios — an if–then plan in action.
Delay all planting until the rains are steady
Reduces false-start risk but can shorten the season too much.
Double fertiliser to push yields while rains last
Adds cost and risk without water; wrong lever in a dry season.

steps.s: An insurer offers rainfall-index cover. A member asks if all losses are paid.
o: Yes, it pays out on any crop loss you suffer
Misleading: payouts follow the index, not each farm's actual loss.
Explain the trigger and basis risk with examples
Honest explanation lets members decide with eyes open.
Tell them insurance is not worth the premium cost
