steps.s: A carbon project offers payments for shade trees with a 30-year contract.
o: Get independent advice on obligations first
Complex, long contracts need independent review before signing.
Sign quickly before the offer closes
Pressure plus complex terms is a classic risk; obligations may outlast benefits.
Let only the chairman's farm join as a test
Testing is sensible, but the contract terms still need review.

modules.d: A practical plan integrating advisory, business management and climate risk for your farm or organisation.
modules.body:
Bringing it together

Your capstone is a practical AI plan for your farm, cooperative, agribusiness or extension programme. It should combine field advisory, business management and climate risk planning, using tools that fit your context and with clear verification and data safeguards.

Plan components

  1. Profile: who you are, crops or livestock, location, scale, members or clients, devices, languages and connectivity.
  2. Challenges and goals: the three most important problems (for example disease losses, low prices, lack of records, climate risk) and measurable goals.
  3. Advisory workflow: how diagnosis and agronomic advice will be obtained and verified — tools, photo protocol, extension links and IPM principles.
  4. Business workflow: record-keeping system, gross margin and cost of production analysis, marketing strategy and finance plan.
  5. Climate and risk plan: weather information sources, seasonal if–then plans, diversification, savings and insurance.
  6. Tool set: selected tools with evaluation scores and costs.
  7. Data and safety rules: farmer data rights, consent, pesticide and veterinary safety, verification with authorities.
  8. Inclusion: how women, youth and less-connected farmers will benefit.
  9. Implementation and measurement: 6–12 month plan with responsibilities and indicators — yields, losses, incomes, costs, adoption and satisfaction.
Start small, measure, expand. Choose one season and one or two priority workflows. Measure carefully against the previous season, learn, and then expand. Many agricultural technology projects fail by trying too much at once.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit your AI plan (no more than six pages), one completed gross-margin and cost-of-production analysis, and one seasonal if–then plan. Your mentor reviews it for practicality, safety, inclusion and local fit.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my agribusiness AI plan coach. Using my profile, challenges and goals, draft a plan with the nine components from this module in under six pages. Include a gross-margin and cost-of-production table template, a seasonal if–then plan, inclusion measures, and a one-season pilot with indicators compared with last season. Flag everything I must verify with extension services, authorities or lenders.

Going deeper — capstone playbook: your Farm/Agribusiness AI Plan

The best agricultural plans are modest, seasonal and measured. Reviewers look for safe advisory practice (especially with pesticides and veterinary products), real numbers from your farm or cooperative, and tools that work on the phones and networks your farmers actually have.

Step-by-step timeline.

  • Week 1 — Profile and baseline. Record crops or livestock, area, last season's yields, costs, prices and losses. Survey members' phones, languages and connectivity.
  • Week 2 — Advisory and tools. Choose and test tools (advisory app, weather service, price information); write the photo protocol and the rule for confirming diagnoses with an extension officer or agro-dealer before any chemical use.
  • Week 3 — Business and climate. Complete the gross-margin and cost-of-production analysis and the seasonal if–then plan; identify insurance or savings options available locally.
  • Week 4 — Plan and present. Set indicators, responsibilities and a 6–12 month timeline; present to your mentor or cooperative leadership.

Deliverables checklist.

  • ☐ AI plan (≤ 6 pages)
  • ☐ Baseline data sheet from last season
  • ☐ Gross-margin and cost-of-production analysis
  • ☐ Seasonal if–then plan
  • ☐ Tool evaluation table with costs
  • ☐ Data, consent and safety rules

Assessment rubric (weighted).

  • Practicality for context — 25%: fits real devices, languages, budgets and skills
  • Agronomic and safety soundness — 20%: verification of advice; safe pesticide and veterinary practice
  • Business analysis — 20%: accurate margins, costs and market plan
  • Climate and risk planning — 15%: clear triggers and responses
  • Inclusion and measurement — 20%: women, youth and less-connected farmers; credible indicators
Worked mini-example. A 60-member maize and soybean cooperative in the Adamawa Region plans one season: farmers send photos of suspected fall armyworm damage to a lead farmer who checks them with an advisory app and confirms with the extension officer before any treatment; weekly prices are collected from two markets and shared in a voice note in Fulfulde and French; members record costs in a simple notebook template that the secretary enters into a spreadsheet. The gross-margin analysis shows transport is a large share of costs, so the cooperative plans group transport. Indicators: losses from pests, price received versus market average, and the number of members keeping records.

Common failure modes.

  • Choosing smartphone-only tools when most members have basic phones.
  • Acting on an AI diagnosis by spraying without confirmation or safety equipment.
  • No baseline, so improvement cannot be measured.
  • Plans for the whole value chain at once instead of one or two workflows.
  • Leaving out women farmers, who may have less access to phones and meetings.

Submission and presentation structure.

  • 1. Who we are and our three priority problems
  • 2. Advisory workflow and safety rules
  • 3. Business numbers and market plan
  • 4. Climate and risk plan
  • 5. Indicators, timeline and support needed
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as an experienced agricultural extension officer and farm business adviser in [country/region]. Here is my farm or cooperative profile and last season's numbers: [paste]. Check my gross-margin calculation for errors, suggest three low-cost ways to improve the margin, and draft a seasonal if–then plan for late rains and a pest outbreak. Mark anything that must be confirmed with a local extension officer.

📚 Glossary

  • If–then plan: pre-planned actions for different scenarios
  • Pilot season: first season testing new workflows before expansion
  • Inclusion measures: actions ensuring benefits reach women, youth and less-connected farmers

📖 References

  • FAO — Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook; farm business guides.
  • CABI Plantwise; PlantVillage.
  • IRAD and MINADER, Cameroon.

quiz.q: A cocoa cooperative in Ntui drafts its AI plan. It wants to launch diagnosis, records, market prices and insurance for all 1,200 members this season. What does the module advise?
opts: Pilot one or two priority workflows for a season, measure against last season, then expand
Launch all four workflows at once so members see the full value of the plan this season
Launch all four workflows for a small group of 50 members, then scale to everyone next year
Delay the plan until funding is secured for every workflow across all 1,200 of the members
quiz.x: Start small with one or two workflows and measure. A 50-member pilot of all four is a reasonable runner-up but still tries too much at once.

quiz.q: A capstone plan for a maize cooperative in Garoua sets goals: 'use AI more and help farmers'. How should the mentor advise revising them?
opts: Keep the goals general so that the cooperative can adapt them during the season
Make goals measurable, e.g. cut storage losses by a set percent versus last season
Replace the goals with a list of AI tools the cooperative intends to buy this year
Add more goals covering every value-chain stage so that the plan looks comprehensive
quiz.x: The plan requires measurable goals and indicators compared with the previous season. Flexible general goals cannot be measured.

quiz.q: A vegetable agribusiness near Yaoundé finished a pilot. Yields rose 10%, but only 20% of women suppliers used the app. Which plan component needs attention?
opts: Climate and risk plan: add seasonal forecasts to raise yields further next season
Tool set: replace the app with a newer one that has higher evaluation scores
Business workflow: add gross margin analysis so that yield gains turn into income
Inclusion: how women, youth and less-connected suppliers will benefit from it
quiz.x: Low adoption by women is an inclusion issue. A new tool might help but does not address the access barriers behind low uptake.

quiz.q: A cooperative's capstone sets indicators for its pilot season. Which set best matches the module?
opts: Yields and incomes for the pilot farmers alone, measured at the end of this season
Number of app downloads, messages sent and training sessions held during the season
Yields, losses, incomes, costs, adoption and satisfaction against last season
Number of tools purchased, total budget spent and number of staff trained on them
quiz.x: The module lists yields, losses, incomes, costs, adoption and satisfaction against last season. Pilot-only yields lack a baseline and miss losses, costs and adoption.

quiz.q: A US-funded programme in Cameroon wants a capstone plan for an extension service. The draft is 18 pages. What should the coach recommend?
opts: Cut to six pages or fewer, plus one gross-margin analysis and one if-then plan
Keep 18 pages, since detailed plans are more convincing to donors and lenders
Cut to two pages and drop the gross-margin analysis so boards read the summary
Split it into three 6-page plans, one for each region, to keep each one short
quiz.x: The capstone is at most six pages plus the analysis and if-then plan. Two pages without the analysis drops a required deliverable.

quiz.q: A cooperative's plan includes a WhatsApp diagnosis service. Which element belongs in its 'data and safety rules' component?
opts: Lead farmers decide which members get access to the service based on their past yields
Members consent to data use, and pesticide or vet advice is verified before it is acted on
Messages are deleted weekly to save phone storage, and members choose any chemical they like
Members agree to send all farm photos to the platform so the AI keeps improving its model
quiz.x: Data and safety rules cover consent, data rights and pesticide/veterinary verification. Mandatory photo sharing ignores consent.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian extension officer is checking a trainee's capstone outline. Which pairing correctly matches a plan component to its content?
opts: Climate and risk plan: record-keeping system and cost of production analysis
Business workflow: weather sources, if-then plans and insurance coverage
Profile: tool evaluation scores, costs and selected providers for the plan
Advisory workflow: tools, photo protocol, extension links and IPM rules
quiz.x: The advisory workflow covers diagnosis tools, photo protocol, extension links and IPM. The other pairings mix up components.

quiz.q: A mentor reviews a coffee cooperative's plan. It relies on a chatbot for fertiliser rates with no soil testing or extension check. Which review criterion is weakest?
opts: Presentation: the plan should include more charts to make the chatbot use clearer
Safety and local fit: advice must be checked locally, not taken from generic AI
Practicality: the plan is too short and needs more workflows to be useful to members
Inclusion: the plan should give chatbot access to women and youth before anyone else
quiz.x: Mentors review for practicality, safety, inclusion and local fit; unverified generic fertiliser rates fail local fit. More workflows would make the plan less practical, not more.

quiz.q: Smallholder farms number about 500 million worldwide. A Nigerian start-up and a Cameroonian cooperative both want plans that scale. Which design choice best supports scale?
opts: Tools that work on basic phones and are delivered through groups and cooperatives
Tools built for the latest smartphones, assuming that handset upgrades will follow
Tools that require each farmer to attend a multi-day training before using them
Tools designed first for large estates, with smallholder versions to follow later
quiz.x: Plans that work on basic phones and through groups match smallholder reality at scale. Designing for estates first misses most farmers.

quiz.q: After one pilot season, a cooperative's records show diagnosis use cut cocoa losses by 15% but price SMS had no effect on sale prices. What should it do next?
opts: Repeat the same pilot unchanged next season to confirm the results before acting
Drop both services, since one of the two workflows failed to show results this season
Expand diagnosis; review why price SMS failed before changing or dropping it
Expand both services, since one success suggests the plan as a whole is working well
quiz.x: Start small, measure, learn, then expand what works. Repeating unchanged delays scaling a proven result and learns nothing about the failure.

facts.t: Components of the capstone AI plan, from profile to measurement.
facts.more: Profile, challenges and goals, advisory, business, climate and risk, tool set, data and safety rules, inclusion, and implementation with indicators.

facts.t: Maximum length of the capstone plan.
facts.more: Plus one gross-margin and cost-of-production analysis and one seasonal if–then plan. Short plans get read and used by cooperative boards and lenders.

facts.t: Recommended pilot length before expanding.
facts.more: Compare against the previous season on yields, losses, incomes, costs, adoption and satisfaction. Many agritech projects fail by doing too much at once.

facts.t: Approximate number of small farms worldwide.
facts.more: IFAD and FAO commonly cite around 500 million smallholder farms. Plans that work on basic phones and through groups scale to this reality.
